/SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 435 PM MDT Fri Oct 9 2026

The stagnant warm and dry weather pattern will finally break on 
Sunday as a powerful upper level low approaches the area from the 
west. A complex interaction will take place between the approaching 
trough, which will be in the process of splitting, and the remnant 
moisture/circulation of former Hurricane Rachel. The best synoptic 
forcing for consistent rainfall will stall to our west, which has 
resulted in a drier trend for much of our area in the last few 
forecast cycles. That being said, we will still have abundant 
moisture in place over the area. Ensemble mean precipitable water is 
around 3 to 4 standard deviations above the mean, near 
climatological maximums. Still, with weak forcing and unimpressive 
instability, precipitation expectations are on the low side. Rawlins 
and Douglas, which will be closest to the strongest forcing, have 
ensemble median QPF values only around 0.1 to 0.2" for the first 
phase of this event which will last through Monday morning. Further 
east, expect a few showers Sunday into Sunday night, but 
precipitation should be fairly limited. In addition to the showers, 
gusty southwest winds will continue along and west of the Laramie 
range. Probabilities for high winds peak around 30% in the wind 
prone areas on Monday morning, but expect fairly consistent gusty 
winds all the way through at least Monday. 

Meanwhile, the northern branch of the split trough will drop a 
surface high pressure down from the north. The surface front will 
push into the area Sunday, but stall around the Laramie range. As a 
result, we can expect a significant cool down for our northern 
areas, solidly behind the front, with Sunday's highs around 15 
degrees cooler than Saturday. The front will struggle to reach the I-
80 corridor, so 24-hour temperature drops in this area will be only 
around 5 degrees or so with highs remaining well above average. The 
upper level low digging into the west coast will help amplify the 
downstream ridge over the central CONUS on Monday, helping to push 
drier air a little further north into our area. Expect a bit more 
sunshine Monday with temperatures around 5 to 10F above seasonal 
norms. A few isolated showers will be possible, but once again, do 
not expect much rainfall. 

Precipitation potential looks more promising during the middle part 
of the week. The now closed upper level low over the west coast will 
push northeastward and eject into the Plains mid-week. This will 
deliver two additional windows for precipitation, both of which look 
better (if you want rainfall) compared to the first phase on 
Sunday/Monday. The "dry" (relatively) slot moves out as another 
surge in southwest flow and mid to upper level moisture pushes 
precipitable water back to around the 97.5 percentile by the end of 
the day Tuesday.  Look for scattered showers developing across the 
area Tuesday continuing into Wednesday, supported by potent 
isentropic lift ahead of the primary trough axis. There is a little 
bit of uncertainty concerning the timing of the trough axis, 
but expect this to push through sometime between Wednesday and 
Thursday morning. There is also potential for a back-edge round 
of precipitation behind the upper level low, forced by the 
development of a TROWAL. The question for this period of time is
how quickly does the system eject, and does it merge back with 
the primary flow to our north before passing through our area. 
This will determine exactly how the back edge of precipitation 
develops, and the potential for high winds (more likely the 
faster the closed low rejoins the parent trough). Overall, the 
second and third phase of this event look more promising in 
ensemble QPF, but there are a lot of ways for these ingredients 
to fail to come together and cause our area to miss out on 
rainfall. Current ensemble median QPF is around 0.5 to 0.75" for
most of the area, but changes are nearly guaranteed as we get 
closer to the event. Relatively few ensemble members (perhaps 
25%) have enough cold air with this system to drop snow levels 
into populated areas of southeast Wyoming, but some light snow 
about 9000 ft in elevation appears likely. We will get a cool 
down with this system regardless of the precise outcome. The 
most likely scenario brings temperatures back to near seasonal 
norms on Tuesday and Wednesday, and then possibly below seasonal
norms for Thursday and Friday. A freeze is likely (50 to 75% 
probability) for Douglas, Rawlins, and Laramie by Friday 
morning, and possible (20 to 50%) for remaining portions of the 
area.
